paper.title: CyFM: Cylindrical Optimal Transport for Few-Step Complex-Valued Flow Matching
paper.abstract: Abstract Complex-valued signals, such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and audio spectrograms, are almost always modelled as flat two-channel Euclidean data. For nonzero values the amplitude–phase chart z ↦ ( | z | , z / | z | ) z\mapsto(|z|,z/|z|) identifies the signal domain with the cylinder ( 0 , ∞ ) × S 1 (0,\infty)\times S^{1} , on which we deliberately replace the inherited metric d ​ A 2 + A 2 ​ d ​ θ 2 dA^{2}+A^{2}d\theta^{2} by the decoupled product metric d ​ A 2 + d ​ θ 2 dA^{2}+d\theta^{2} . In this empirical study we measure what that substitution costs and what it buys. By computing exact analytical bridges, we demonstrate that Cartesian paths induce a heavy-tailed distribution of angular velocity (power law index ≈ 1.0 \approx 1.0 ), with nearly half of the probability paths exceeding an angular speed of π \pi under independent coupling, a rate no cylindrical path ever exceeds. To resolve this, we analyze Cylindrical Flow Matching (CyFM), which strictly bounds the regression target, and couple noise and data by exact minibatch Optimal Transport computed jointly over whole fields in the cylindrical metric. Although the transport-cost reduction of this coupling collapses with field dimension (from 86 % 86\% for scalar pairs to 3 % 3\% for 64 × 64 64\times 64 fields), its benefit to few-step generation does not: it lowers the few-step error of the cylindrical model by 3 3 – 60 % 60\% at every evaluated resolution. With this coupling, CyFM has a lower error than the best Cartesian baseline at every step count up to k = 8 k=8 and every evaluated resolution, with all five seeds separated and without distillation, and at convergence we detect no significant difference between the two geometries. Finally, we expose the “Factorized Coupling Trap,” showing that dimension-wise or patch-wise transport factorizations silently destroy the joint distribution of the data. All experiments are on synthetic complex fields.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Flow Matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) has emerged as a state-of-the-art paradigm for continuous-time generative modeling, offering simulation-free training and straightforward extension to Riemannian manifolds ( Chen & Lipman, 2024 ; Mathieu & Nickel, 2020 ) . Interest has recently grown in applying these methods to complex-valued physical signals z = x + i ​ y = A ​ e i ​ θ ∈ ℂ z=x+iy=Ae^{i\theta}\in\mathbb{C} , such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) or Audio Spectrograms, where the signal phase θ \theta encodes critical structural and physical properties. However, existing frameworks almost universally force complex signals into a naive Euclidean embedding: the data is treated as a two-channel flat Cartesian vector ( Re ⁡ ( z ) , Im ⁡ ( z ) ) ∈ ℝ 2 (\mathrm{Re}(z),\mathrm{Im}(z))\in\mathbb{R}^{2} . As illustrated in Figure 1 , the plane itself is perfectly well behaved; what suffers is the probability path drawn on it. Straight Euclidean probability paths z ⁡ ( t ) = ( 1 − t ) ​ z 0 + t ​ z 1 z(t)=(1-t)z_{0}+tz_{1} obey the triangle inequality, which pulls intermediate states below the amplitude of either endpoint, and arbitrarily close to the origin when the phases are near-antipodal. Furthermore, the phase of a Cartesian path can turn arbitrarily fast when the endpoints are close to antipodal. The Cartesian target z 1 − z 0 z_{1}-z_{0} is itself bounded whenever the endpoints are; what is unbounded is the rate at which the path turns, and that is what a coarse integrator has to resolve. (a) Standard Euclidean Flow ( ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} ) (b) Cylindrical Flow Matching (Ours) Figure 1: Geometric mismatch in complex-valued generative flows. (a) In the Euclidean complex plane ( Re ⁡ ( z ) , Im ⁡ ( z ) ) (\mathrm{Re}(z),\mathrm{Im}(z)) , linear probability trajectories pass close to the origin, inducing severe midpoint amplitude attenuation ( | z 1 / 2 | ≪ 1 2 ​ ( | z 0 | + | z 1 | ) |z_{1/2}|\ll\frac{1}{2}(|z_{0}|+|z_{1}|) ). (b) Cylindrical Flow Matching works in amplitude–phase coordinates on ( 0 , ∞ ) × S 1 (0,\infty)\times S^{1} under the decoupled product metric, transporting phase along the minimal circular geodesic while preserving amplitude. Prior work in representation learning and abstract feature alignment has proposed decoupled metrics on cylindrical or polar product manifolds to alleviate these issues ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . However, attempting to scale these Riemannian formulations to raw, high-dimensional complex wavefields introduces entirely new failure modes associated with spatial coherence and empirical Optimal Transport (OT). In this paper, we conduct an empirical analysis of Euclidean versus Cylindrical Flow Matching for complex-valued synthesis. While our target physical domains of interest are complex MRI and audio, we isolate the fundamental geometric mechanisms by evaluating on synthetic complex fields with known ground-truth distributions. We define Cylindrical Flow Matching (CyFM) on the product manifold ℳ = [ 0 , ∞ ) × S 1 \mathcal{M}=[0,\infty)\times S^{1} with a decoupled product metric, whose target angular velocity is bounded by construction ( | u θ | ≤ π |u_{\theta}|\leq\pi ), and measure on exact analytical probability paths what the Cartesian alternative costs. We couple noise and data by exact minibatch OT computed jointly over whole fields in the cylindrical metric, and find that although its transport-cost reduction collapses as the field dimension grows, its benefit to few-step generation persists. Finally, we expose the “Factorized Coupling Trap”—a common but flawed countermeasure where transport plans are factored per-dimension or per-patch, which we show destroys the joint distribution. Contributions. • Bridge geometry. We measure, on exact probability paths, how fast the phase has to turn. The Cartesian bridge has a heavy tail with power-law index ≈ 1 \approx 1 , which we derive in closed form for equal amplitudes: under independent coupling, nearly half of its paths exceed an angular speed of π \pi , the bound the cylindrical target never crosses at any coupling. • Few-step generation. At 16 × 16 16\times 16 , 32 × 32 32\times 32 and 64 × 64 64\times 64 , CyFM with the joint coupling reaches a lower error than the best Cartesian baseline at every k ≤ 8 k\leq 8 integration steps, with all five seeds separated and no distillation. Run to convergence, we detect no significant difference between them. • Joint OT at field scale. We couple noise and data by exact minibatch OT over whole fields in the cylindrical metric. Its saving in transport cost shrinks as the field grows, from 86% on scalar pairs to 3% for 64 × 64 64\times 64 fields (batch 64). The few-step error of the cylindrical model still drops by 3–60% at every resolution we evaluated. • The factorized coupling trap. Factorizing that coupling per coordinate (amplitude/phase) or per patch is the obvious way around the cost of OT in high dimension. It quietly destroys the target instead. The marginals survive intact, the dependence between them does not, and structural coherence across patch seams goes with it.

sections.heading: 2.1 Flow Matching on Euclidean and Riemannian Manifolds
sections.text: Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs) parameterize generative transformations between a tractable base distribution and a target data distribution via time-dependent ordinary differential equations (ODEs) ( Chen et al., 2018 ) . Flow Matching (FM) ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) broke the historical computational bottleneck of CNFs by directly regressing a neural vector field onto closed-form target paths, enabling simulation-free training. Subsequent advances incorporated minibatch optimal transport couplings ( Pooladian et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) to straighten probability trajectories and reduce inference latency. Recognizing that physical and structural data frequently inhabit non-Euclidean spaces, Riemannian Flow Matching (RFM) ( Chen & Lipman, 2024 ) extended vector field regression to general Riemannian manifolds. Recently, the specific polar or cylindrical decoupled manifold construction ( ℝ + × S d − 1 \mathbb{R}^{+}\times S^{d-1} ) has been explored in representation learning and abstract feature alignment. For instance, Direct Product Flow Matching (DP-FM) ( Chen et al., 2026 ) applies a decoupled metric to Vision-Language Model latent features to resolve angular dynamics distortion during few-shot adaptation, while DisRFM ( Wang et al., 2026 ) utilizes polar Riemannian flows for structure-preserving graph domain adaptation. However, applying this geometric construction directly to raw, high-dimensional complex wavefields (e.g., D = 4096 D=4096 ) presents unique scaling challenges regarding spatial coherence and optimal transport, which remain largely unexplored.

sections.heading: 2.2 Deep Generative Models for Complex-Valued Signals
sections.text: The processing of complex-valued physical wavefields, such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) or Audio STFTs, inherently requires modeling both magnitude and phase ( Bernstein et al., 2004 ; Trabelsi et al., 2018 ) . While supervised networks have successfully adopted complex convolutions ( Cole et al., 2021 ) , modern generative frameworks (such as Score-Based Diffusion Models ( Song et al., 2021 ; Chung & Ye, 2022 ) ) almost universally operate strictly on real-valued magnitude images, or naively treat real and imaginary parts as two Cartesian channels in ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} , inheriting the metric of the plane. Very recently, a few works have begun exploring generative models for complex signals. Schlimbach et al. (2026) combine a complex-valued variational autoencoder with latent flow matching for brain MRI, and model the phase in a learned Euclidean latent space rather than on its circular domain. Other works, such as PhaseGen ( Rempe et al., 2025 ) for MRI or UniverSR ( Choi et al., 2025 ) for audio, similarly default to Euclidean formulations. As we demonstrate in this paper, Cartesian interpolation structurally induces origin singularities and extreme angular velocities.

sections.heading: 2.3 Optimal Transport Traps in Flow Matching
sections.text: Minibatch optimal transport (OT) is commonly used to pair noise and data in flow matching ( Pooladian et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) . Related couplings under a Riemannian cost have been used on other manifolds: FoldFlow-OT ( Bose et al., 2024 ) for protein backbones on SE ​ ( 3 ) N \mathrm{SE}(3)^{N} , and Metric Flow Matching ( Kapuśniak et al., 2024 ) with geodesics of a learned, data-induced metric. Three aspects distinguish our setting from prior work: the modality consists of complex-valued fields; the manifold is ( [ 0 , ∞ ) × S 1 ) H × W ([0,\infty)\times S^{1})^{H\times W} , whose phase factor is a circle at every pixel; the research question: how the coupling behaves as the field dimension grows and why it must not be factorized. The population-level coupling induced by minibatch OT, as well as its dependence on batch size, has recently been characterized by Boïté et al. (2026) . Because minibatch OT scales at least quadratically with the batch, cheaper couplings have been proposed: One-Sided Quantile Coupling (QC-FM, Kim et al., 2026 ) constructs each source sample from one-dimensional rank statistics of the data along random projections, leaving every data sample intact. A different shortcut, which we show must be avoided, factorises the coupling itself: matching coordinates (amplitude and phase) or spatial patches with independent permutations. This reassembles data samples out of parts of different samples and destroys the joint data distribution (Section 5 ).

sections.heading: 4 Cylindrical Flow Matching
sections.text: To remove the amplitude factor from the phase geometry, we formulate Cylindrical Flow Matching (CyFM) for complex-valued fields. A crucial conceptual clarification is that CyFM constructs the full signal domain as a decoupled product manifold of local voxel manifolds: ℳ H × W = ∏ u = 1 H ∏ v = 1 W ℳ u , v = ( [ 0 , ∞ ) × S 1 ) H × W . \mathcal{M}^{H\times W}=\prod_{u=1}^{H}\prod_{v=1}^{W}\mathcal{M}_{u,v}=([0,\infty)\times S^{1})^{H\times W}. (9) The fundamental group of a product is the product of the factors’, and each factor is homotopy equivalent to S 1 S^{1} , so π 1 ​ ( ℳ H × W ) = ℤ H ​ W \pi_{1}(\mathcal{M}^{H\times W})=\mathbb{Z}^{HW} : every pixel wraps independently of the others. This product structure has three consequences: • Point-wise Separability: The product Riemannian metric g = ∑ u , v ( d ​ A u , v 2 + d ​ θ u , v 2 ) g=\sum_{u,v}(dA_{u,v}^{2}+d\theta_{u,v}^{2}) decomposes completely point-wise. Geodesics, exponential maps, and logarithmic maps require zero spatial inter-pixel coupling in the probability paths, making them embarrassingly parallel. • Vanishing Curvature: Because each local factor is intrinsically flat (Gaussian curvature K = 0 K=0 ), the entire product manifold ℳ H × W \mathcal{M}^{H\times W} has identically vanishing Riemann curvature ( R ≡ 0 R\equiv 0 ), so the construction carries no curvature-dependent local terms. This is not an advantage over the Cartesian baseline, which is flat as well, and flatness removes neither the 2 ​ π 2\pi wrap, nor the cut locus at antipodal phase, nor the boundary at A = 0 A=0 . • Architectural Synergy: Spatial correlations are learned by the neural network backbone, while the geometric probability path bounds the target angular velocity ( | u θ | ≤ π |u_{\theta}|\leq\pi ) at every spatial coordinate.

sections.heading: 4.2 Joint Optimal Transport Coupling on the Cylinder
sections.text: Pairing prior and data samples independently yields crossing conditional paths whose average the network must regress. Minibatch Optimal Transport (OT) ( Pooladian et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) reduces this by re-pairing each training batch. CyFM performs this re-pairing jointly over whole fields in the cylindrical metric. For a batch of prior fields { x 0 i } i = 1 B \{x_{0}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{B} and data fields { x 1 j } j = 1 B \{x_{1}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{B} , the cost of pairing i i with j j is the squared norm of the cylindrical logarithmic map, averaged over all pixels and both tangent components: c i ​ j = 1 2 ​ H ​ W ​ ∑ u = 1 H ∑ v = 1 W [ ( A 1 , u ​ v j − A 0 , u ​ v i ) 2 + w ​ d S 1 ​ ( θ 0 , u ​ v i , θ 1 , u ​ v j ) 2 ] , c_{ij}=\frac{1}{2HW}\sum_{u=1}^{H}\sum_{v=1}^{W}\Big[\big(A^{j}_{1,uv}-A^{i}_{0,uv}\big)^{2}+w\,d_{S^{1}}\big(\theta^{i}_{0,uv},\theta^{j}_{1,uv}\big)^{2}\Big], (14) with phase weight w = 1 w=1 and d S 1 d_{S^{1}} the geodesic (wrapped) angular distance. At every training step the permutation σ \sigma minimising ∑ i c i ​ σ ​ ( i ) \sum_{i}c_{i\sigma(i)} is found exactly by linear sum assignment, and the geodesic bridge of the previous subsection is built between x 0 i x_{0}^{i} and x 1 σ ⁡ ( i ) x_{1}^{\sigma(i)} . Generation is unaffected: it starts from the prior and integrates the learned field. The assignment is joint: amplitude, phase and all pixels of a field are moved together, so every data sample stays intact and the coupling is a valid transport plan between the joint distributions. Because the metric is a sum over coordinates, it is tempting to factorise the problem into independent one-dimensional sorts per coordinate or per spatial patch; this destroys the joint target distribution (Section 5.4 ).

sections.heading: 4.3 Continuous Trigonometric Embedding
sections.text: Two discontinuities meet here, and only one of them is an artefact. The scalar angle θ ∈ [ − π , π ) \theta\in[-\pi,\pi) jumps across the negative real axis ( − π ∼ π -\pi\sim\pi ); where that jump sits depends only on where the interval is cut, and any faithful representation of S 1 S^{1} removes it. Passing raw scalar angles directly to neural networks introduces sharp gradients at this branch cut. The second discontinuity is intrinsic: every point of S 1 S^{1} has a cut locus at its antipode, where the two minimal arcs have equal length π \pi and the sign of u θ u_{\theta} is arbitrary, so the logarithmic map is discontinuous there. sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We organise the evaluation around four claims. First, we show through analytical bridges that the cylindrical target has no origin singularity. Second, we verify the practical interaction of this geometry with U-Net architectures and Optimal Transport. Third, we ablate the framework across spatial dimensions to test scaling robustness and the effect of the joint OT coupling. Fourth, we show that factorising the coupling destroys the joint target distribution.

sections.heading: 5.4 The Factorized Coupling Trap
sections.text: Because the cylindrical metric is a sum over amplitude and phase, and over pixels, it is tempting to solve the transport problem separately per coordinate or per spatial patch. The factorised minimum is always a lower bound on the joint one, and it is attained exactly when some joint plan is simultaneously optimal in every coordinate — which holds when both distributions are product measures, and degenerately when source and target coincide, but not in general. We measure the consequence without any network, on the pointwise copula target (spiral structure) with n = 1024 n=1024 pairs and 8 seeds (Table 4 ). Coupling amplitude and phase independently leaves both marginals bit-identical to the target (Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance 0 0 ), yet the circular-linear correlation of the coupled data falls to ≈ 0.04 \approx 0.04 at every ρ \rho , and its transport cost stays flat at 0.20 0.20 while the true optimum rises to 0.38 0.38 at ρ = 1 \rho=1 : the factorised plan reports a cost below the optimum because it no longer transports the target. The spatial analogue behaves identically. On 64 × 64 64\times 64 fields (correlation length 6), coupling 16 × 16 16\times 16 patches independently leaves the pooled sliced W 2 W_{2} to the data at 0.000 0.000 and the correlation inside patches at 0.979 0.979 , but the lag-1 correlation across patch seams falls from 0.979 0.979 to 0.044 0.044 . The damage is in the coupled targets themselves: a factorised plan reassembles endpoints from different data samples, so the law that the flow-matching objective transports to at its population optimum is that reassembled law and not the data. sections.heading: 5.5 Scope and Future Work
sections.text: All results in this paper are on synthetic complex fields. The next steps are: evaluating on physical signals, namely unconditional generation of complex MRI images (fastMRI, Zbontar et al., 2018 ) and complex audio spectrograms; adding spatial metrics alongside the pooled sliced W 2 W_{2} ; and investigating the Cartesian geometry’s lower phase error at intermediate step counts.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this empirical study, we compared Euclidean and cylindrical geometries for complex-valued generative Flow Matching. On exact probability paths, Cartesian interpolation produces a heavy-tailed angular velocity near the origin, while mapping complex fields onto the decoupled cylindrical manifold ( [ 0 , ∞ ) × S 1 [0,\infty)\times S^{1} ) bounds the target angular velocity by π \pi . On synthetic fields up to 64 × 64 64\times 64 , Cylindrical Flow Matching (CyFM) with the joint coupling has a lower error than the Cartesian baselines at every step count up to k = 8 k=8 , without distillation, and shows no significant difference at convergence. Our analysis also found two limits in scaling such flows to fields. First, the transport-cost reduction of minibatch Optimal Transport collapses at field scale, yet the joint cylindrical coupling still lowers the few-step error of CyFM at every resolution. Second, the Factorized Coupling Trap arises when the coupling is factorized across coordinates or spatial patches. This factorization destroys the joint data distribution. We also found that the training objective matters: an amplitude-weighted ℒ 1 \mathcal{L}_{1} loss leaves the flow-matching fixed point, and under it the cylindrical model fell behind at convergence and did not improve reliably with more integration steps; the squared error removes both. What remains open is the Cartesian geometry’s lower phase error at intermediate step counts. Explaining it, and evaluating on physical signals, is the next step.

For nonzero values the amplitude–phase chart z ↦ ( | z | , z / | z | ) z\mapsto(|z|,z/|z|) identifies the signal domain with the cylinder ( 0 , ∞ ) × S 1 (0,\infty)\times S^{1} , on which we deliberately replace the inherited metric d ​ A 2 + A 2 ​ d ​ θ 2 dA^{2}+A^{2}d\theta^{2} by the decoupled product metric d ​ A 2 + d ​ θ 2 dA^{2}+d\theta^{2} . In this empirical study we measure what that substitution costs and what it buys. By computing exact analytical bridges, we demonstrate that Cartesian paths induce a heavy-tailed distribution of angular velocity (power law index ≈ 1.0 \approx 1.0 ), with nearly half of the probability paths exceeding an angular speed of π \pi under independent coupling, a rate no cylindrical path ever exceeds. To resolve this, we analyze Cylindrical Flow Matching (CyFM), which strictly bounds the regression target, and couple noise and data by exact minibatch Optimal Transport computed jointly over whole fields in the cylindrical metric. Although the transport-cost reduction of this coupling collapses with field dimension (from 86 % 86\% for scalar pairs to 3 % 3\% for 64 × 64 64\times 64 fields), its benefit to few-step generation does not: it lowers the few-step error of the cylindrical model by 3 3 – 60 % 60\% at every evaluated resolution. With this coupling, CyFM has a lower error than the best Cartesian baseline at every step count up to k = 8 k=8 and every evaluated resolution, with all five seeds separated and without distillation, and at convergence we detect no significant difference between the two geometries. Finally, we expose the “Factorized Coupling Trap,” showing that dimension-wise or patch-wise transport factorizations silently destroy the joint distribution of the data. All experiments are on synthetic complex fields. 1 Introduction Flow Matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) has emerged as a state-of-the-art paradigm for continuous-time generative modeling, offering simulation-free training and straightforward extension to Riemannian manifolds ( Chen & Lipman, 2024 ; Mathieu & Nickel, 2020 ) . Interest has recently grown in applying these methods to complex-valued physical signals z = x + i ​ y = A ​ e i ​ θ ∈ ℂ z=x+iy=Ae^{i\theta}\in\mathbb{C} , such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) or Audio Spectrograms, where the signal phase θ \theta encodes critical structural and physical properties. However, existing frameworks almost universally force complex signals into a naive Euclidean embedding: the data is treated as a two-channel flat Cartesian vector ( Re ⁡ ( z ) , Im ⁡ ( z ) ) ∈ ℝ 2 (\mathrm{Re}(z),\mathrm{Im}(z))\in\mathbb{R}^{2} . As illustrated in Figure 1 , the plane itself is perfectly well behaved; what suffers is the probability path drawn on it. Straight Euclidean probability paths z ⁡ ( t ) = ( 1 − t ) ​ z 0 + t ​ z 1 z(t)=(1-t)z_{0}+tz_{1} obey the triangle inequality, which pulls intermediate states below the amplitude of either endpoint, and arbitrarily close to the origin when the phases are near-antipodal. Furthermore, the phase of a Cartesian path can turn arbitrarily fast when the endpoints are close to antipodal. The Cartesian target z 1 − z 0 z_{1}-z_{0} is itself bounded whenever the endpoints are; what is unbounded is the rate at which the path turns, and that is what a coarse integrator has to resolve. (a) Standard Euclidean Flow ( ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} ) (b) Cylindrical Flow Matching (Ours) Figure 1: Geometric mismatch in complex-valued generative flows. (a) In the Euclidean complex plane ( Re ⁡ ( z ) , Im ⁡ ( z ) ) (\mathrm{Re}(z),\mathrm{Im}(z)) , linear probability trajectories pass close to the origin, inducing severe midpoint amplitude attenuation ( | z 1 / 2 | ≪ 1 2 ​ ( | z 0 | + | z 1 | ) |z_{1/2}|\ll\frac{1}{2}(|z_{0}|+|z_{1}|) ). (b) Cylindrical Flow Matching works in amplitude–phase coordinates on ( 0 , ∞ ) × S 1 (0,\infty)\times S^{1} under the decoupled product metric, transporting phase along the minimal circular geodesic while preserving amplitude. Prior work in representation learning and abstract feature alignment has proposed decoupled metrics on cylindrical or polar product manifolds to alleviate these issues ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . However, attempting to scale these Riemannian formulations to raw, high-dimensional complex wavefields introduces entirely new failure modes associated with spatial coherence and empirical Optimal Transport (OT). In this paper, we conduct an empirical analysis of Euclidean versus Cylindrical Flow Matching for complex-valued synthesis. While our target physical domains of interest are complex MRI and audio, we isolate the fundamental geometric mechanisms by evaluating on synthetic complex fields with known ground-truth distributions. We define Cylindrical Flow Matching (CyFM) on the product manifold ℳ = [ 0 , ∞ ) × S 1 \mathcal{M}=[0,\infty)\times S^{1} with a decoupled product metric, whose target angular velocity is bounded by construction ( | u θ | ≤ π |u_{\theta}|\leq\pi ), and measure on exact analytical probability paths what the Cartesian alternative costs. We couple noise and data by exact minibatch OT computed jointly over whole fields in the cylindrical metric, and find that although its transport-cost reduction collapses as the field dimension grows, its benefit to few-step generation persists. Finally, we expose the “Factorized Coupling Trap”—a common but flawed countermeasure where transport plans are factored per-dimension or per-patch, which we show destroys the joint distribution. Contributions. • Bridge geometry. We measure, on exact probability paths, how fast the phase has to turn. The Cartesian bridge has a heavy tail with power-law index ≈ 1 \approx 1 , which we derive in closed form for equal amplitudes: under independent coupling, nearly half of its paths exceed an angular speed of π \pi , the bound the cylindrical target never crosses at any coupling. • Few-step generation. At 16 × 16 16\times 16 , 32 × 32 32\times 32 and 64 × 64 64\times 64 , CyFM with the joint coupling reaches a lower error than the best Cartesian baseline at every k ≤ 8 k\leq 8 integration steps, with all five seeds separated and no distillation. Run to convergence, we detect no significant difference between them. • Joint OT at field scale. We couple noise and data by exact minibatch OT over whole fields in the cylindrical metric. Its saving in transport cost shrinks as the field grows, from 86% on scalar pairs to 3% for 64 × 64 64\times 64 fields (batch 64). The few-step error of the cylindrical model still drops by 3–60% at every resolution we evaluated. • The factorized coupling trap. Factorizing that coupling per coordinate (amplitude/phase) or per patch is the obvious way around the cost of OT in high dimension. It quietly destroys the target instead. The marginals survive intact, the dependence between them does not, and structural coherence across patch seams goes with it. 2 Related Work 2.1 Flow Matching on Euclidean and Riemannian Manifolds Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs) parameterize generative transformations between a tractable base distribution and a target data distribution via time-dependent ordinary differential equations (ODEs) ( Chen et al., 2018 ) . Flow Matching (FM) ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) broke the historical computational bottleneck of CNFs by directly regressing a neural vector field onto closed-form target paths, enabling simulation-free training. Subsequent advances incorporated minibatch optimal transport couplings ( Pooladian et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) to straighten probability trajectories and reduce inference latency. Recognizing that physical and structural data frequently inhabit non-Euclidean spaces, Riemannian Flow Matching (RFM) ( Chen & Lipman, 2024 ) extended vector field regression to general Riemannian manifolds. Recently, the specific polar or cylindrical decoupled manifold construction ( ℝ + × S d − 1 \mathbb{R}^{+}\times S^{d-1} ) has been explored in representation learning and abstract feature alignment. For instance, Direct Product Flow Matching (DP-FM) ( Chen et al., 2026 ) applies a decoupled metric to Vision-Language Model latent features to resolve angular dynamics distortion during few-shot adaptation, while DisRFM ( Wang et al., 2026 ) utilizes polar Riemannian flows for structure-preserving graph domain adaptation. However, applying this geometric construction directly to raw, high-dimensional complex wavefields (e.g., D = 4096 D=4096 ) presents unique scaling challenges regarding spatial coherence and optimal transport, which remain largely unexplored. 2.2 Deep Generative Models for Complex-Valued Signals The processing of complex-valued physical wavefields, such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) or Audio STFTs, inherently requires modeling both magnitude and phase ( Bernstein et al., 2004 ; Trabelsi et al., 2018 ) . While supervised networks have successfully adopted complex convolutions ( Cole et al., 2021 ) , modern generative frameworks (such as Score-Based Diffusion Models ( Song et al., 2021 ; Chung & Ye, 2022 ) ) almost universally operate strictly on real-valued magnitude images, or naively treat real and imaginary parts as two Cartesian channels in ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} , inheriting the metric of the plane. Very recently, a few works have begun exploring generative models for complex signals. Schlimbach et al. (2026) combine a complex-valued variational autoencoder with latent flow matching for brain MRI, and model the phase in a learned Euclidean latent space rather than on its circular domain. Other works, such as PhaseGen ( Rempe et al., 2025 ) for MRI or UniverSR ( Choi et al., 2025 ) for audio, similarly default to Euclidean formulations. As we demonstrate in this paper, Cartesian interpolation structurally induces origin singularities and extreme angular velocities. 2.3 Optimal Transport Traps in Flow Matching Minibatch optimal transport (OT) is commonly used to pair noise and data in flow matching ( Pooladian et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) . Related couplings under a Riemannian cost have been used on other manifolds: FoldFlow-OT ( Bose et al., 2024 ) for protein backbones on SE ​ ( 3 ) N \mathrm{SE}(3)^{N} , and Metric Flow Matching ( Kapuśniak et al., 2024 ) with geodesics of a learned, data-induced metric. Three aspects distinguish our setting from prior work: the modality consists of complex-valued fields; the manifold is ( [ 0 , ∞ ) × S 1 ) H × W ([0,\infty)\times S^{1})^{H\times W} , whose phase factor is a circle at every pixel; the research question: how the coupling behaves as the field dimension grows and why it must not be factorized. The population-level coupling induced by minibatch OT, as well as its dependence on batch size, has recently been characterized by Boïté et al. (2026) . Because minibatch OT scales at least quadratically with the batch, cheaper couplings have been proposed: One-Sided Quantile Coupling (QC-FM, Kim et al., 2026 ) constructs each source sample from one-dimensional rank statistics of the data along random projections, leaving every data sample intact.
